Power or Nah

2026Personal projectSole author · published on GitHub

A pocket-sized IoT device that shows whether electricity is cheap or expensive — right now. Built on an M5StickC Plus 2, it pulls Finnish spot prices directly from the ENTSO-E API, classifies them against the day's own distribution using percentile thresholds, and glows green, blue, orange, or red accordingly. No app, no subscription, no friction.

Working device — running daily
View on GitHub The device The challenge

Finnish electricity prices swing dramatically throughout the day — a price of 3 c/kWh at 2 am might be rock-bottom cheap, while the same 3 c/kWh at 6 pm could be one of the cheapest hours available. Absolute numbers are meaningless without context. Most electricity apps require unlocking a phone, opening a tab, and mentally comparing against remembered averages. The goal was a device that answers one question — is now a good time to use electricity? — at a glance, from across the room.

The approach

The firmware fetches the ENTSO-E day-ahead price XML for the Finnish bidding zone (10YFI-1--------U) each minute, parses all 15-minute intervals for the current day, and sorts them to compute four percentile thresholds on the fly. The current price is classified against those thresholds — not against a fixed table. This means a day where all prices are high still shows CHEAP for the cheapest hours, and a day with very low prices does not mislead you into thinking 2 c/kWh is expensive.

// Dynamic thresholds — recalculated from today's sorted prices
tCheap = percentile(todayPrices, count, 0.30);
tOkay = percentile(todayPrices, count, 0.55);
tExpensive = percentile(todayPrices, count, 0.80);
tPain = percentile(todayPrices, count, 0.95);

// Classify current price relative to today
if (c < 0.0) return NEGATIVE;
if (c <= tCheap) return CHEAP;
if (c <= tOkay) return OKAY;
if (c <= tExpensive) return EXPENSIVE;
return PAIN;
Key capabilities

Relative pricing

Thresholds are recalculated each fetch from the day's own prices — cheap means cheap today, not against a fixed baseline that becomes outdated as the energy market shifts.

Cheapest hour ahead

Button A shows the single cheapest upcoming price and its time window — useful when you can defer running the dishwasher or charging an EV by a couple of hours.

Today's context

Button B shows the day's price range and the exact threshold values — so you can see at a glance whether today is generally a cheap or expensive day.

No cloud middleman

The device talks directly to the ENTSO-E public API — no third-party server, no account, no subscription. It just needs a WiFi connection and a free API token.

Key outcomes

Always-on awareness

Sitting on a shelf, the device communicates electricity price context passively — no phone, no app, no action required to stay informed.

Smarter consumption habits

A quick glance before running a high-load appliance is enough. Over time it shifts energy use toward off-peak hours without any planning effort.

End-to-end ownership

From API parsing and XML manipulation on an ESP32 to percentile maths in C++ — every part of the stack was written and debugged from scratch.
